cells.tense: Present tense — you're here, holding it.
cells.verb: tending what's in your care, keeping more than one need fed without dropping either
cells.place: from the spot where you can see how all of it fits together
cells.ask: let one person see what the tending has actually cost you, and let one thing you've finished growing stay finished — care that doesn't wear you out comes back when the carrying is witnessed and the done things are allowed to be done.
cells.core:
You can see the whole of what you're looking after, and you're looking after it. Not one corner at the expense of another — you hold two needs at once and keep both fed, and you do it with your hands, in the practical details, not from a distance. Nobody has to tell you where it's thin; you already see it, and you've already moved toward it.

What this is free to feed next is simpler than it sounds: being seen doing it. Letting someone know what it has taken. And letting one finished thing be finished — set down because it's complete, not because you gave up on it.
cells.sheetLine: You see all of it and you're tending all of it, by hand.

cells.tense: Future tense — bracing for a season that hasn't come.
cells.verb: over-tending, adjusting every part of what's in your care before anything has asked for it
cells.place: from the spot where you can see the whole picture, which keeps showing you more to fix
cells.ask: before you add one more safeguard, picture one thing in your care already fully grown — and stay with how that would feel for a minute. Care that doesn't exhaust comes back when you can imagine it finished instead of only threatened.
cells.core:
You see the whole of it, and that's become the problem: every place it could go wrong is visible, so you're already there, tending it. Watering what isn't dry. Shoring up what hasn't cracked. Somewhere ahead is a version where you finally have every part handled, and you're living there, which means you're never quite here where things are, in fact, mostly growing.

The care is real. It's just running ahead of the thing it's caring for, and it's starting to cost you more than any of it would cost to lose.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending every outcome before it's happened.

cells.tense: Past tense — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: seeing what needs tending and leaving it untended
cells.place: from the spot where you can see the whole picture, including what you've stepped back from
cells.ask: don't push yourself back into the caretaking. Instead, name one thing in all of this you still want to see grow — and let yourself keep wanting it, out loud if you can. Holding without clutching comes back when the hoping is alive again, not when the hands are forced.
cells.core:
You can still see it all. You know what's thin, what's overdue, what would take ten minutes of attention — and you're not giving it. Something behind you made the tending feel pointless, or like it cost more than it returned, and you're still taking direction from that moment. The seeing didn't stop. The caring-for did.

It won't come back by making yourself tend. It comes back from the other side: from wanting something in this to grow again, and letting that want be real before you lift a finger.
cells.sheetLine: You see what needs looking after and you've stopped looking after it.

cells.tense: Disowned present — you're already keeping it going, and calling it something else.
cells.verb: quietly tending what's in your care, balancing the needs of it without saying so
cells.place: from the spot where you can see the whole picture, and talk as if the picture holds itself together
cells.ask: tell one person, plainly, that you've been the one keeping this going — and then let one piece of it be done, finished because you finished it. Care that doesn't clutch comes back when the intent behind it is visible, starting with you.
cells.core:
The whole thing holds together, and it holds together because of you. You see where it's thin and you feed it. You keep two needs alive at once without anyone noticing a choice was made. And when it's mentioned, you say it just works out, or someone had to, or it isn't really anything.

It is something. The tending is happening every day. The only person not giving you credit for it is the one doing it — and as long as that's true, nothing you've grown gets to be finished, because nobody's allowed to see it was grown.
cells.sheetLine: You're the reason it holds. You keep saying it just does.
